# Gold Slips as Markets Await Fed Chairman Comments at Jackson Hole

Aug. 25, 2026 8:36 pm ET

* * *

Listen

(57 sec)

0034 GMT — Gold declines in Asian trade. Markets appear to be waiting for [Federal Reserve](https://www.wsj.com/topics/subject/federal-reserve) chairman [Kevin Warsh](https://www.wsj.com/topics/person/kevin-warsh) to clarify his views on when the central bank is likely to react to inflation when he speaks at the annual Jackson Hole gathering Friday, say ANZ Research analysts in a note. A higher interest rate environment typically weighs on nonyielding assets such as gold. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also didn’t offer further signals on any changes to the country’s debt management, after last week’s announcement around bond buybacks revived concerns over U.S. fiscal policy and the dollar’s weakness, ANZ adds. Spot gold falls 0.2% to $4,646.77 a troy ounce.(megan.cheah@wsj.com)

Gold eased back slightly after hitting a fresh three-month peak, with traders taking a breath ahead of key U.S. inflation numbers and a speech from Federal Reserve Chair [Warsh](https://stockinvest.us/stock/KVNW) due later this week. By early Tuesday, spot gold had dipped about 0.4% to $4,634 an ounce, while futures showed a mild decline.

The recent jump in gold prices largely followed the U.S. Treasury's announcement to potentially double its buyback of longer-dated government bonds. This reversal revived worries about fiscal discipline and the dollar's strength, nudging investors toward traditional hedges like gold.

At the same time, bond yields have softened, reducing the cost advantage of holding non-yielding bullion. The dollar's retreat also made the precious metal cheaper for holders of other currencies, adding to its appeal.

U.S. Treasury Secretary [Scott Bessent](https://stockinvest.us/stock/SCBK) hinted at expanded debt buybacks and mentioned plans for a fiscal strategy aiming to tackle the government's borrowing costs, though he stopped short of offering fresh details on further moves.

Market commentators note that these fiscal maneuvers and the renewed focus on government debt strategy have rekindled what's called the 'debasement trade'-investors aiming to hedge against the risk that rising debt levels and accommodative policies might erode the dollar's purchasing power over time.

The spotlight now turns to Wednesday's release of the core personal consumption expenditures price index, a key inflation gauge closely followed by the Fed. Then on Friday, Chair [Warsh](https://stockinvest.us/stock/KVNW) will deliver remarks at the Federal Reserve's annual meeting in Jackson Hole, which could add more signals about the central bank's rate path.

The geopolitical stage adds another layer of uncertainty. The U.S. is ramping up sanctions against nations conducting business with Iran, while trade frictions with Canada escalated recently, with Washington imposing hefty tariffs on several goods and threatening more on automotive products starting 2027. These developments are stirring debate about gold's role amid escalating geopolitical and trade tensions.

Some analysts see technical charts backing gold's recent rally, suggesting a solid floor was established around $3,942 late last June. Yet the market's reaction to ongoing diplomatic moves-like easing Middle East tensions which might lower oil prices-could test gold's momentum and influence central banks' policy decisions.

With all these factors at play, gold is navigating a complex knot of fiscal concerns, trade disputes, and policy expectations, keeping traders on their toes as they monitor the news flow this week.

# Target Boosts Full-Year Forecast After Strong Q2 Sales and Windfall Tariff Refund

[![](https://cdn.stockinvest.us/blog-stockinvest/2024/03/twistedemporus_usiness_journalistmale_adolescent_mid-30s_real_l_76563fb7-7ea8-4ac6-a833-424444791f0d-99fe83.png)Lukas Schmidt](https://stockinvest.us/digest/author/lukas-schmidt)

[![](https://stockinvest.us/storage/logos/corporate.target.com.png)-3.78%](https://stockinvest.us/stock/TGT)

![](https://stockinvest.us/storage/blog/image?image=blog-stockinvest%2F2026%2F08%2FimageForEntry3-2jf-07ec80.webp&w=1000)

Target [TGT](https://stockinvest.us/stock/TGT) shook off some of the sluggishness that's been dogging its business by delivering a solid second quarter. The retailer reported net sales up 5.3% year over year, with same-store sales rising 3.8% - outperforming the 2.4% analysts had predicted.

A sizable chunk of Target's earnings surge came from a $752 million tariff refund that padded its bottom line. That unexpected windfall translated into a $994 million pre-tax bump, inflating the company's quarterly gross margin and operating income.

CEO Michael Fiddelke didn't sugarcoat it: while this quarter shows real progress, Target is far from finished turning its business around. He's calling Q2 an important milestone, yet acknowledges there's plenty of ground to cover to sustain momentum and drive long-term growth.

Shining amid the numbers was an 8.7% jump in digital comparable sales, fueled by an impressive 25% increase in same-day delivery. These gains highlight Target's evolving omni-channel strategy and efforts to engage customers where they want to shop.

On the product line front, food and beauty categories posted solid gains, contributing to the "broad-based" sales strength the company emphasized. However, apparel and home goods lagged and remain areas that Target plans to revamp, with refreshed assortments aimed at wooing shoppers back into these segments.

Price cuts also featured heavily in Target's strategy - more than 10,000 items saw reductions during the quarter, with further markdowns expected. This aggressive approach is part of its plan to drive traffic and respond to consumers who are increasingly cautious with spending.

The company also expanded its footprint by opening 17 new stores, signaling ongoing confidence in its brick-and-mortar presence despite rising e-commerce trends.

Thanks to these developments, Target raised its full-year sales growth forecast from 4% to about 5%. Earnings per share guidance, inclusive of the tariff refund, moved up to a range of $9.90 to $10.90, while the outlook excluding that one-time gain sits between $8.25 and $9.25 per share.

Shareholders didn't exactly throw a party - premarket trading saw shares dip roughly 4% as investors weighed the one-off nature of the tariff boost against the operational improvements. With consumers still battling inflation and economic uncertainty, the real test will be if Target can keep this up beyond the tariff tailwind.
